newsitem.title: USA: California affirmative action rule hits law school.
newsitem.headline: California affirmative action rule hits law school.

text.p: The University of California at Berkeley's Boalt Hall law school Wednesday reported a sharp drop in minority admissions in its first class without affirmative action.
The prestigious law school's dean, Herma Hill Kay, said the drop was "precisely what we feared would result from the elimination of affirmative action at Boalt."

The law school said 14 black students were admitted for this fall's entering class, down from 75 students last year. Hispanic and Puerto Rican student admissions dropped to 16 from 34, while admissions of Native Americans dropped to just two students from nine last year.

Admissions, in contrast, soared for white and Asian students. A total of 538 white students were admitted, up from 467 last year, the university said. The number of Asians and Pacific Islanders admitted rose to 149 from 126 last year.
The University of California's governing board of regents decided in 1995 to ban affirmative action in student admissions. The rule took effect at Boalt this year.
Kay warned that the university's policy would dramatically change the law school.

"The students and faculty at Boalt Hall have obtained great educational benefit from the racial diversity of our student body," she said. "I deeply regret that Boalt's offers of admission to minority applicants have dropped so sharply."

The university's ban on admissions preferences was strongly supported by California's Republican Gov. Pete Wilson, who favours rolling back affirmative action policies used since the 1960s to increase opportunities for racial minorities and women.
Last November, Californians approved Proposition 209, which bans state and local government affirmative action programmes in public employment, education and contracting.
